items.t: SSE Composite Today: Shanghai Falls to 3,634.35 as AI Hardware Slumps and ChiNext Drops 3.32% Amid Nvidia's Turmoil
sum: Mainland Chinese stocks opened higher but slid in the afternoon as optical-module and circuit-board makers sold off on Nvidia’s leadership turmoil, while banks hit record highs and kept the Shanghai benchmark well ahead of Shenzhen.

The Shanghai Composite Index closed at 3,634.35 points on Friday 13 November 2026, down 21.48 points or 0.59%. It was the index’s second straight decline after a 0.67% fall to 3,655.83 on Thursday, and it left the benchmark back below its five-day and ten-day moving averages. The session range ran from 3,623.84 to 3,669.44.

The headline loss understates the damage across the wider market. The Shenzhen Component Index fell 2.05% to 10,968.79, the growth-focused ChiNext Index slid 3.32% to 2,426.08, the STAR 50 lost 2.30% to 1,279.66 and the blue-chip CSI 300 eased 0.68% to 4,016.29. More than 4,700 stocks declined against roughly 750 that rose, and combined Shanghai and Shenzhen turnover shrank to about 1.66 trillion yuan, around 276 billion yuan less than on Thursday.

A-shares opened higher and the Shanghai Composite traded in positive territory through the morning, briefly rising about 0.2% towards 3,663. The tone changed sharply after the lunch break, when selling hit the computing-hardware complex and the index fell almost 1% at its worst before trimming losses into the close.

The dominant story of the session was the abrupt exit of Jensen Huang, the co-founder who had led Nvidia since 1993. The company said on Thursday that he had stepped down as president, chief executive and board member with immediate effect, following reports of multiple affairs, including one with a woman US intelligence suspects of spying for China. Chief financial officer Colette Kress is serving as interim CEO, Harvey C. Jones becomes the company’s first independent chairman, and Nvidia is due to report quarterly results next week. Nvidia shares opened as much as 14% lower on Thursday before closing down 4.34%, and extended losses on Friday after HSBC downgraded the stock.

Chinese suppliers of optical modules, printed circuit boards and electronic components have been among the biggest beneficiaries of US AI data-centre spending, so the uncertainty around Nvidia’s strategy hit them hardest.

sum: Investing.com -- Chinese artificial intelligence stocks came under renewed pressure on Friday as Nvidia's leadership crisis heightened fears that Washington could tighten restrictions on China's access to advanced AI computing.
The selloff hit major developers including Z.AI, MiniMax, Tencent and Alibaba, as investors assessed the risk that they could lose access to Nvidia-powered processors through overseas data centres.
Nvidia shares fell as much as 14% on Thursday after co-founder Jensen Huang resigned, but dip-buyers narrowed the decline to 4.3% by the close.

The company confirmed that Chief Financial Officer Colette Kress would take over as interim CEO while its board searches for a permanent replacement. Nvidia shares slipped another 3% in extended trading.
Hong Kong-listed Z.AI plunged 10.88% and MiniMax dropped 8.73% in the latest market snapshot. Tencent fell 2.71%, while Alibaba declined 2.35% and Kuaishou Technology lost 3.91%.
Hong Kong's Hang Seng slipped 0.9%, while mainland China's CSI 300 fell 0.1% and the Shanghai Composite edged up 0.2%, after mainland benchmarks had advanced over the previous three sessions.

The pressure reflects concern that Nvidia's turmoil could accelerate efforts in Washington to close a gap in existing export controls. Although the U.S. restricts direct exports of its most advanced AI processors to China, Chinese companies have been able to rent computing capacity remotely through overseas data centres.

sum: Investing.com -- Asian stocks were mixed on Wednesday as semiconductor shares rallied in Japan, South Korea and Taiwan, while Hong Kong and Chinese technology stocks came under pressure.

Who keeps crashing China’s stock market?
items.s: macau daily times 澳門每日時報
sum: China is scrambling to contain a stock-market rout only two years after the previous rescue.

Beijing is dusting off the market-support playbook it deployed in 2024. The People’s Bank of China is providing low-cost funding for corporate share buybacks and liquidity for institutional investors. The shadowy “national team” appears to have stepped up its operations, while regulators are again resorting to window guidance — informally instructing institutional investors and brokerages not to sell.

In October, China’s stock market suffered its worst monthly decline in more than a decade. The blue-chip CSI 300 Index has fallen into a bear market from its late-June peak, while Shanghai’s semiconductor-heavy SSE Science and Technology Innovation Board 50 Index, or Star 50, has plunged as much as 48%.

Liang certainly has reason to deflect blame. China has a long history of faulting private-sector investors, from quant funds to foreign asset managers, for igniting selloffs. But he might just have a point this time.

China had already endured a bear market in July, when momentum-driven trades suffered their worst loss in history. The pattern mirrored markets in South Korea and the US, where the red-hot semiconductor trade was hastily unwound. Three months later, however, the usual suspects are harder to blame. Margin financing has already fallen, as has northbound turnover through the Stock Connect with Hong Kong, suggesting neither leveraged traders nor foreign hot money is behind the latest weakness. That leaves a different potential offender: long-only institutional investors.

State-owned insurers have been steadily increasing their stock holdings in recent years. China Life Insurance Co., for instance, has scaled up artificial-intelligence-related bets and raised its equity allocation to 19.2% of its portfolio by the end of June, from 16.9% in 2025. Beyond the hunt for higher returns, insurers have been responding to policymakers, who want them to provide more long-term capital to the stock market — a priority that the head of China’s securities regulator reiterated in a high-profile speech in mid-June. Talk about bad timing.

Stock Futures Tick Up as Traders Await Inflation Data and AI Earnings
sum: Stock futures demonstrated a slight uptick on Sunday evening as traders remained focused on the potential recovery of technology shares. Anticipation was building for the upcoming inflation data and earnings reports from major artificial intelligence companies scheduled for the week ahead. Specifically, S&P 500 futures recorded a gain of 0.1%, while the Nasdaq 100 futures increased by 0.3%. Additionally, futures tied to the Dow Jones Industrial Average saw an increase of 101 points, equivalent to 0.2%.

Over in Asia, markets exhibited mostly positive performance on Monday, with Taiwanese equities leading the charge. The Taiwan Weighted Index surged nearly 5%, buoyed by a significant rebound in key stocks such as TSMC and Hon Hai Precision Industry, widely recognized as Foxconn. The Nikkei 225 in Japan climbed by 3.25%, while the Topix index increased by 3.44%, largely supported by gains in financial and consumer cyclical stocks. South Korea’s Kospi index rose by 1.15%, overcoming an initial decline, whereas the small-cap Kosdaq index dipped by 0.23%. Major tech companies Samsung Electronics and SK Hynix experienced gains of 2.49% and 2.03%, respectively. In Hong Kong, the Hang Seng Index rose 1.03%, while the CSI 300 index in mainland China was up by 0.3%.

Investors in Asia were also focused on October inflation data from China, which revealed the producer price index reaching its highest point in over four years at 5.7%. In contrast, consumer inflation came in slower than anticipated at 0.7%. Meanwhile, Australia’s S&P/ASX 200 faced a decline of 0.51%.

The preceding Friday had witnessed a partial rebound from Thursday’s significant selloff driven by AI-related concerns, as chip stocks experienced renewed buying interest. The tech-heavy Nasdaq Composite rose by 1.09% to 24,579.42, and the broad-market S&P 500 increased by 0.31% to 7,376.86. Conversely, the blue-chip Dow Jones Industrial Average fell by 237.33 points, or 0.46%, ending at 51,285.73. Broader investor sentiment remained cautious amidst stronger-than-expected jobs data, and concerns persisted following robust midterm election results for Democrats.

Bloomberg: Investors shift to China and India after AI stock sell-off
sum: Following a broad sell-off in AI stocks, investors began reallocating capital to previously out-of-favor markets in China and India. Fund managers are looking for opportunities in sectors less dependent on AI infrastructure, Bloomberg reported.

The shift in strategy followed the U.S. midterm elections, in which Democrats gained control of both chambers of Congress. Bloomberg said market participants feared tighter AI regulation and reassessed the payback of multibillion-dollar investments in data centers. Against this backdrop, on November 5 the Nasdaq Composite fell 5.52%.

The next day, following U.S. indexes, Japan’s Nikkei 225 and South Korea’s KOSPI fell by about 6%. Asian technology shares came under the most pressure. Samsung Electronics, SK Hynix and Taiwan Semiconductor Manufacturing supply equipment for AI infrastructure, so their business largely depends on spending by U.S. corporations.

For the week, India’s Nifty 50 gained 8.6%, its best performance since February 2021. The Sensex rose 8.8%. Reuters noted that on November 6 both indexes closed at their highest levels in more than eight months.

The rally was fueled by foreign inflows. According to Bloomberg, over the four days through November 4, foreign investors put about $1.9 billion into Indian equities. During the next trading session, funds’ net purchases reached $1.6 billion — the highest one-day total in nearly six years.

Bloomberg also cited the structure of India’s stock market: AI hardware makers have a relatively small weight in local indexes. Charlie Hong, investment director at LOGOS Asset Management, told Bloomberg that in October he sold SK Hynix, Samsung Electronics, Intel and Lumentum. He increased allocations to Indian technology companies, financials and drug manufacturers.
Banks led gains. According to Reuters, India’s financial sector added 10.4% for the week, HDFC Bank rose 13.8%, and ICICI Bank gained 12.4%.

sum: HONG KONG: China and Hong Kong stocks fell on Friday as a Nasdaq-led tech rout rippled across Asia and fuelled fears the AI boom is losing steam, although bargain hunting helped pare losses in mainland markets buoyed by Beijing’s market-supporting measures.
China’s blue-chip CSI 300 Index dropped 1.4 percent, but notched up a 1.7 percent gain for the week to snap a 12-week-long losing streak.
The Shanghai Composite Index fell 1.1 percent on Friday, though it ended the week 1.4 percent higher, breaking a six-week run of declines.

In Hong Kong, the benchmark Hang Seng Index was down 1.3 percent but registered a 5.1 percent weekly gain, its best since March 2025. The Hang Seng Tech Index slid 1.8 percent on Friday, but posted its best weekly gain since February 2025, advancing 8.6 percent.

Tech sectors across Asia took a heavy blow after a steep selloff overnight in the US wiped trillions of dollars off market value, as investors fretted that a Democratic sweep in the US midterm elections could bring tighter scrutiny of the AI sector.
China’s tech-focused Star 50 Index and the AI Index slumped as much as 5.2 percent before paring some losses.
Dong Baozhen, chairman of asset manager Lingtong Shengtai, said the overnight slump in US tech stocks meant the logic behind the AI-driven rally had crumbled.

South Korea's Stock Market Plummets Amid Concerns Over AI and Oil Prices
sum: The sell-off of tech stocks in the U.S. is also weighing on stock markets in Asia. The South Korean stock market has been particularly hard hit. Trading in Seoul had to be temporarily suspended.
The South Korean stock market has come under massive pressure amid a global sell-off of tech stocks. As a result, the benchmark KOSPI index plummeted by more than 8 percent in early trading.

Shares of memory chip manufacturers SK Hynix (-11 percent) and Samsung Electronics (-8 percent) also fell sharply. Due to the sharp price declines, the Seoul Stock Exchange suspended trading for 20 minutes. A so-called “circuit breaker” is designed to prevent panic selling from further destabilizing the market.

Investors appeared to be reacting to the losses on Wall Street, where concerns about the future of investment in artificial intelligence weighed on stock prices. This comes against the backdrop of the Democrats’ victory in the U.S. midterm elections, which heightened fears of a possible slowdown in the expansion of data centers. Due to their high financing requirements and potential environmental damage, the expansion of new data centers in the United States is facing increasing resistance.

In addition, the South Korean news agency Yonhap cited the risk of rising oil prices as another reason for the market declines, following reports from Iran that several tankers had once again been damaged in the Strait of Hormuz. As an energy-poor industrialized nation, South Korea is heavily reliant on oil imports from the Middle East. At the same time, its stock market is particularly vulnerable to fluctuations in the AI sector due to the semiconductor industry’s significant weight in the market.

Japan's leading index, the Nikkei 225, fell by about 6.5 percent in early trading. The Hang Seng Index in the Hong Kong Special Administrative Region fell by about 1.3 percent shortly after the market opened, while the CSI 300 Index, which tracks the 300 leading stocks on China’s mainland stock exchanges, dropped by about 1.7 percent.

sum: Efforts stepped up to bolster capital market liquidity and stability

China's financial regulators are stepping up efforts to bolster capital market liquidity and stability, with the central bank preparing a fresh round of funding support for institutional investors and the securities regulator moving to encourage more share buybacks and attract additional long-term capital.

The People's Bank of China announced on Monday that it would conduct a new round of operations under its securities, funds and insurance companies swap facility (SFISF) on Tuesday to support the sound and stable development of the capital market.

The move will have a one-year tenor, with possible extensions, the PBOC said in a statement. So far, 31 securities and fund management firms have applied for more than 100 billion yuan ($15 billion) under the operation.

Introduced in 2024, the facility allows eligible securities firms, fund managers and insurers to swap assets including bonds, stock exchange-traded funds and CSI 300 Index constituent shares for highly liquid assets such as government bonds and central bank bills.
The funds obtained should be used exclusively for capital market investments, including stock and stock ETF investments and market-making.

Lou Feipeng, a researcher at Postal Savings Bank of China, said the new SFISF operation will provide nonbanking financial institutions with liquidity support that can help break the vicious cycle of redemptions and forced sell-offs, facilitating countercyclical share purchases during market downturns without expanding the monetary base.

sum: - China’s central bank will meet securities and banking regulators and major banks on Monday to study improving a relending scheme for share buybacks, local media said, after the CSI 300 fell 8.5% in October in its worst month in more than a decade.

Monday’s session in mainland China and Hong Kong is the first chance for equities to react to the reports, and the prospect of state-backed support may help sentiment at the open after October’s heavy selling. Whether that lasts is likely to depend on detail. Traders have already seen last month’s measures fail to halt the slide, so the scale and terms of any expanded relending facility will matter more than the signal alone. A credible support package could also ease some pressure on the yuan and on broader Asian risk appetite. Without concrete steps, the combination of contracting PMIs and doubts over AI earnings leaves the downside case in place.
After a record losing streak in Chinese stocks, Beijing appears to be reaching for more support tools, though last month showed that a signal on its own is not enough. Info via Bloomberg (gated).

items.t: SSE Composite Falls to 3,599.02, a New 52-Week Closing Low, as October Losses Reach 6.33% Amid Geopolitical Tensions
sum: Mainland Chinese stocks extended a technology-led slide on Friday 30 October 2026, with the Shanghai benchmark posting its lowest close since August 2025 and the CSI 300 recording a record 12th straight weekly decline.

The Shanghai Stock Exchange Composite Index closed at 3,599.02 on Friday 30 October 2026, down 52.42 points or 1.44% from Thursday's close of 3,651.43, according to figures reported by Xinhua and confirmed by Morningstar's Dow Jones Market Data. The index opened roughly 1.3% lower near 3,605 and spent the session under pressure, closing just below the psychologically important 3,600 level.

The close marks a new 52-week closing low for the benchmark and its lowest finish since 4 August 2025. Friday's loss came on top of a 0.82% decline on Thursday, meaning the index has dropped more than 2.2% across the final two sessions of the month.

The immediate catalyst was a global retreat from artificial intelligence and semiconductor shares after Amazon and Intel released disappointing quarterly updates in the United States. Intel warned of a weak fourth quarter on the back of a slump in personal computer demand, while Amazon's results and holiday-quarter guidance missed expectations. These reports followed Alphabet's steep fall on Thursday and deepened doubts about how quickly heavy AI spending will translate into profits.

Mainland China's growth boards are particularly sensitive to that narrative. Computing-power hardware and memory-chip companies, which had attracted heavy domestic retail and institutional buying earlier in the year, were sold aggressively for a second straight day. The pain was far worse outside the main Shanghai board: the ChiNext growth index in Shenzhen plunged about 4.1% on Friday after sinking 4.45% on Thursday.

The SSE Composite, which covers all A and B shares listed in Shanghai and includes a large weighting in banks, energy and state-owned industrials, therefore fell less than the technology-heavy gauges. Even so, losses of this size on a broad, value-tilted index reflect how widely the risk-off mood spread through mainland portfolios.
October was the SSE Composite's weakest month in a considerable time. The index lost 243.18 points, or 6.33%, during the month, according to Dow Jones Market Data.
